title: The Moon
sources: NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day, Apollo 17's Lunar Rover (apod.nasa.gov)

cover.artAlt: A giant full moon rising over a calm dark ocean with stars in the sky
cover.blurb: It is the only other world people have ever stood on. Turn the page and go there.

pages.title: Footprints That Never Wash Away
pages.artAlt: A crisp astronaut bootprint pressed into gray moon dust

facts.text: The bootprints the astronauts left are still up there. The Moon has almost no air, so there is no wind and no rain to blow them away or wash them out.

The gray powder they stepped in is called regolith. It is rock that meteorites smashed into dust, and up close every speck is rough and jagged, like a tiny chip of broken glass. It clings to boots and gloves instead of brushing off like beach sand.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a gloved astronaut hand holding a scoop of fine gray moon dust, with grains clinging all over the white glove
facts.caption: Moon dust clings to everything it touches.

infographic.title: How the Moon got its dust

stops.label: Space rocks crash into the Moon, over and over, for a very long time
The crashes break the ground into a fine powder full of sharp, jagged bits
A boot presses in, and with no wind or rain to wipe it away the print just stays

infographic.caption: There are no numbers to check on this one. It is the story NASA tells of how the Moon's dust was made and why a footprint stays put.

pages.title: Twelve People Have Walked Here
pages.artAlt: An astronaut in a white spacesuit on the gray lunar surface with Earth in the black sky

facts.text: Only twelve people have ever walked on the Moon. They all went during the Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972, starting with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin.
The Moon's gravity is about one sixth of Earth's. If you can hop a step high here, you could hop about six times higher there, which is why the astronauts bounced instead of walked.
facts.artAlt: An astronaut in a white spacesuit caught in the middle of a bounce above the gray lunar ground, both boots up off the surface
facts.caption: One little push, and up you go.

facts.text: The sky above them stayed black even in the middle of the day. Without air to scatter the sunlight, there is no blue sky on the Moon.
facts.artAlt: An astronaut standing in bright white sunlight on the Moon with a completely black sky behind, sharp shadows on the ground
facts.caption: Bright sunshine, and the sky is still black.

infographic.title: How high could you hop on the Moon?

rows.label: Your best hop here on Earth
That same hop on the Moon

infographic.caption: The Moon's gravity, one sixth of Earth's, comes from NASA, and that is what makes the hop six times higher. The hop and the door are everyday sizes, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: A World Full of Craters
pages.artAlt: Close-up of the Moon's surface showing overlapping craters and long shadows

facts.text: Every crater is a scar from something crashing in. Earth gets hit too, but our air burns most rocks up and our weather slowly erases the marks. The Moon keeps every single one.
The biggest one is called the South Pole to Aitken basin, and it is more than 1,550 miles across. That is about the distance from Waco, Texas all the way to Washington, DC.
facts.artAlt: The far side of the Moon seen from space, with the huge shallow bowl of the South Pole to Aitken basin darkening the bottom of the disk
facts.caption: The far side of the Moon, with its giant basin across the bottom.

facts.text: The Moon is roughly a quarter as wide as Earth, and it sits about 239,000 miles away. You could line up about thirty Earths side by side in the gap between us.
facts.artAlt: Earth and the Moon photographed together from far out in space, a big blue and white Earth beside a small gray Moon with black space between them
facts.caption: Earth and the Moon, with all that empty space in between.

infographic.title: How wide is the biggest crater?

rows.label: A drive across the United States
The whole Moon, all the way across
The South Pole to Aitken basin

infographic.caption: The Moon's width and the crater's width both come from NASA. The drive across the country is an everyday distance, here only so you have something to measure against, and it shows that one crater is most of the Moon wide.

pages.title: They Drove a Car on the Moon
pages.artAlt: The lunar rover parked on the Moon's surface with an astronaut nearby

facts.text: The last three Apollo missions carried a battery-powered buggy called the Lunar Roving Vehicle. It folded up like a deck chair to fit on the lander.
The rover was not fast. Its top speed was about 8 miles an hour, roughly the pace of a kid on a bicycle, but it still let the astronauts travel miles from their lander instead of a short walk.
facts.artAlt: An astronaut sitting in the lunar rover driving across the Moon, with two curling arcs of gray dust flying up behind the wheels
facts.caption: The buggy throws up two curling arcs of dust as it rolls.

facts.text: All three rovers are still parked up there. There was no room to bring them home, so they sit exactly where the astronauts left them.
facts.artAlt: The empty lunar rover standing alone on the gray Moon, with wheel tracks leading away across the dust and no one in sight
facts.caption: Still parked, right where the astronauts left it.

infographic.title: How fast was the Moon buggy?

rows.label: The Moon buggy at full speed
A car on a town street

infographic.caption: The buggy's top speed comes from NASA. The walk and the car are everyday speeds, here only so you have something to measure against.

finish.title: You finished The Moon!
finish.blurb: The Moon also pulls on our oceans, and that is what makes the tides go in and out every day. Fold a corner on your favorite page so you can find it again.
